narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, and both pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile after your first year and the bottom decile after your third year, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These low academic standings were the main reasons the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor and worked in your favor, gently pulling the prediction toward passing. At 3.20 it sits only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, so the model saw some solid academic ability.

Your family income bracket (middle) was the third most influential feature and also nudged the outcome slightly toward success, though its effect was smaller.

Taken together, the model concluded that your relatively weak performance in law school coursework outweighed the positive signals from your GPA and background, resulting in a just-over-50% estimated risk of failing the bar.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your class rank in the coming year if possible, consider targeted bar-prep resources early, and retake the LSAT if you can raise your score meaningfully. A stronger academic record and higher LSAT would likely change the prediction in a future application. (248 words)
